hints: Think about which two subshells iron uses for its outer electrons and how much energy it costs to remove an electron from each one.
walkthrough:
Picture where iron's outer electrons live**
Iron is $[\text{Ar}]\ 3\text{d}^{6}\ 4\text{s}^{2}$. That means its outermost electrons are spread across two subshells that are very close together in the energy level diagram, the $4\text{s}$ and the $3\text{d}$.

Link similar energy to variable loss**
Because the $3\text{d}$ and $4\text{s}$ levels are so close in energy, a similar amount of ionisation energy removes electrons from either level. So iron can lose just the $4\text{s}$ electrons to give $+2$, or $4\text{s}$ plus one or more $3\text{d}$ electrons to give $+3$ and higher states.
Final answer: The energies of the $3\text{d}$ and $4\text{s}$ subshells / orbitals are very similar, so electrons can be removed from both with little difference in energy.

hints: Count the total electrons in Fe (26) and in $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ (23), and remember which subshell loses electrons first when a transition metal ionises.
walkthrough:
Write Fe first**
Neutral Fe has atomic number 26. After argon (18 electrons), 8 remain. Fill in energy order: $4\text{s}$ before $3\text{d}$, giving $[\text{Ar}]\ 3\text{d}^{6}\ 4\text{s}^{2}$.

Remove for $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ correctly**
When forming positive ions, always remove $4\text{s}$ electrons before $3\text{d}$. Remove the two $4\text{s}$ electrons first, then one $3\text{d}$ electron: $8 - 3 = 5$ electrons left in d, so $[\text{Ar}]\ 3\text{d}^{5}$.
Final answer: $\text{Fe} = [\text{Ar}]\ 3\text{d}^{6}\ 4\text{s}^{2}$ AND $\text{Fe}^{3+} = [\text{Ar}]\ 3\text{d}^{5}$

hints: Picture $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$ and ask yourself what sits at the centre and what is attached around it.
walkthrough:
Build the mental picture**
Think of $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$. Right in the middle is $\text{Fe}^{3+}$. Around it are six water molecules pointing their lone pairs toward the metal. That central plus surrounding arrangement is the definition.

Use the key terms**
The surrounding water molecules are ligands, bonded by dative covalent bonds. So a complex is a central metal atom or ion with ligands bonded to it.
Final answer: A central metal atom / ion surrounded / bonded by one or more ligands.

hints: Count how many ligand donor atoms are directly bonded to Fe in $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$, remembering water is monodentate.
walkthrough:
Count bonds to the metal**
Coordination number means number of dative bonds to the central metal, which equals number of donor atoms. Each $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ is monodentate and donates one lone pair, and there are six of them, so coordination number is 6.
Final answer: 6 / six

hints: Recall why free water is bent at $104.5^{\circ}$ and think about what changes to repulsion when one oxygen lone pair is no longer fully free but donated to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$.
walkthrough:
Start from free water**
In free $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ oxygen has two bond pairs and two lone pairs. Lone pair repulsion squeezes the H-O-H angle down to $104.5^{\circ}$.

See what coordination does**
When water bonds to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, one oxygen lone pair is donated into the metal to form the Fe-O dative bond. That pair is now shared and held between two atoms, so it repels the O-H bonds less strongly than a free lone pair.

Predict the angle shift**
Less lone pair repulsion lets the two O-H bonds spread out a little, so the angle increases slightly to about $106-108^{\circ}$, still pyramidal at oxygen but closer to tetrahedral.

Final answer: H-O-H angle about $107^{\circ}$ (106-108$^{\circ}$). A lone pair on O is donated to Fe in a dative bond, so it becomes a bonding pair and repels less, allowing the H-O-H angle to open up.

hints: Start from the isolated $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ion where all five d orbitals have the same energy, then think what approaching ligands do to that degeneracy.
Think about what an electron in the lower set of d orbitals can do if light of just the right energy arrives.
Remember the colour you see is not the colour absorbed, think about the relationship between absorbed light and transmitted or reflected light.
walkthrough:
Split the d orbitals**
On its own, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ has five $3\text{d}$ orbitals all at the same energy, we say degenerate. When six ligands approach octahedrally, their lone pairs repel d electrons unequally, so the set splits into a lower energy group and a higher energy group with gap $\Delta E$.

Absorb light to jump the gap**
If a photon has energy exactly equal to $\Delta E$, an electron in the lower d level can absorb it and jump up to the upper level. This is a d-d transition. Only certain wavelengths in the visible region match the gap, so only those colours are absorbed.

See the complementary colour**
White light minus the absorbed colour is what reaches your eye. So the solution appears as the complementary colour of the light absorbed. That is why the complex looks coloured.

Final answer: Ligands cause the (degenerate) $3\text{d}$ orbitals to split into two energy levels / become non-degenerate.
An electron absorbs visible light energy and is promoted to the higher energy level (d-d transition).
Colour seen is the complementary colour to that absorbed.

hints: Compare the two complexes and spot the only difference in the inner coordination sphere, $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ versus $\text{SCN}^{-}$.
Link the strength of the ligand field to the size of the d-orbital gap and then to the energy of light absorbed using $E = hf$.
walkthrough:
Different ligand, different field**
$\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ and $\text{SCN}^{-}$ are different ligands with different field strengths. Replacing one $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ by $\text{SCN}^{-}$ changes how strongly the ligands split the d orbitals, so $\Delta E$ is different for $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$ and $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{5}\text{SCN}]^{2+}$.

Different gap means different colour**
Since $\Delta E = h\nu = hc/\lambda$, a different gap needs a different frequency and wavelength of photon to promote the electron. Different light absorbed means a different complementary colour is left to be seen, for example pale violet versus intense red.

Final answer: Different ligands cause a different d-d energy gap / $\Delta E$ / $\Delta_{\text{oct}}$.
Therefore a different frequency / wavelength of light is absorbed, so a different complementary colour is transmitted / seen.

hints: Track the ligands: one $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ leaves and one $\text{H}_{2}\text{PO}_{4}^{-}$ enters, think where the extra proton from $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ must go.
walkthrough:
Write a ligand substitution**
One water ligand is replaced by dihydrogenphosphate. Balance atoms and charge: left side $3+$ total, right side complex is $2+$, so the displaced water plus the extra $\text{H}^{+}$ from $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ appears as $\text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+}$. Check: Fe 1, O and H and P all balance, charge $3+ = 2+ + 1+$.
Final answer: $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+} + \text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4} \rightarrow [\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{5}(\text{H}_{2}\text{PO}_{4})]^{2+} + \text{H}_{3}\text{O}^{+}$

hints: Write the formation equilibrium for $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{5}\text{SCN}]^{2+}$ from $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$ and $\text{SCN}^{-}$, omitting water as a pure liquid.
Work out units by putting concentration units $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ into your expression, products over reactants.
walkthrough:
Form the expression**
$K_{\text{stab}}$ is the equilibrium constant for complex formation:
$$[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+} + \text{SCN}^{-} \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{5}(\text{SCN})]^{2+} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$
Water is omitted, so:
$$K_{\text{stab}} = \frac{[[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{5}(\text{SCN})]^{2+}]}{[[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}][\text{SCN}^{-}]}$$

Deduce units**
Each concentration is in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$:
$$\text{units} = \frac{\text{mol dm}^{-3}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})(\text{mol dm}^{-3})} = \text{mol}^{-1}\text{dm}^{3}$$

Final answer: $K_{\text{stab}} = \frac{[[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{5}(\text{SCN})]^{2+}]}{[[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}][\text{SCN}^{-}]}$
units = $\text{mol}^{-1}\text{dm}^{3}$

hints: Think of the target equilibrium as formation of the SCN complex minus formation of the phosphate complex, so consider how to combine the two $K_{\text{stab}}$ values.
walkthrough:
Divide the stability constants**
The required $K_{\text{c}}$ is $K_{\text{stab}}(\text{SCN complex}) / K_{\text{stab}}(\text{phosphate complex})$:
$$K_{\text{c}} = \frac{1.30 \times 10^{2}}{5.90 \times 10^{1}}$$
$$K_{\text{c}} = 2.20$$

Comment on value**
$K_{\text{c}} > 1$ shows the equilibrium lies slightly to the right, consistent with the SCN complex being more stable, as its larger $K_{\text{stab}}$ shows.
Final answer: $K_{\text{c}} = 2.20$ (min 2 s.f.)
